cards.back: The broker checks each order, routes it to the exchange and keeps users' books. Only the exchange matches buyers and sellers.

cards.front: Order rate at the market open
cards.back: 15M orders over 22,500 s is about 670 a second; if 20% arrive in the first 15 minutes, about 3,300 a second.

cards.front: Market data fan-out at the open
cards.back: 2M phones × 50 symbols × 1 update a second is 100M ticks a second, about 35 Gb/s at 44 bytes each.
202 once the broker accepts it, not once it trades; the fill arrives later over the WebSocket. An idempotency key makes retried taps safe.
SENT: on the wire with an unknown result. Never resend blindly; reconnect, replay the session from its last sequence number and ask for status.

cards.front: Why the risk system is partitioned by account
cards.back: One thread per account partition checks margins in memory one order at a time: no locks, no double spending, microsecond checks, backed by a replicated log.
The best price fills first; at the same price, the older order fills first.

cards.front: Which price does a crossing order pay?
cards.back: The resting order's price. A buy at ₹412.60 against an ask at ₹412.55 pays ₹412.55.

cards.front: Why one matching thread per symbol
cards.back: Orders are handled strictly in sequence from a log, so results are deterministic and replaying the log rebuilds the exact book.
The ticker plant publishes snapshots on a timer, collapsing hundreds of ticks a second into one message per symbol. The single biggest saving.

cards.front: How a gateway handles a slow phone
cards.back: It keeps only the latest snapshot per symbol per socket and overwrites it, so the phone skips stale prices instead of building a queue.
T+1: a Monday trade settles Tuesday. Until then a share is a position shown as T1, then a holding in the demat account.

quiz.q: The exchange link drops right after an order is sent, and the broker doesn't know if it arrived. What should it do?
choices: Mark it rejected and refund margin
Reconnect, replay the session from the last sequence number and ask for the order's status
Ask the user to place it again
quiz.why: Resending from SENT could buy twice; unknown is not failed.

quiz.q: Two orders from one account arrive a millisecond apart, and together they exceed available margin. What prevents both being accepted?
choices: The account's single-threaded RMS partition blocks margin for the first before checking the second
A database row lock per order
quiz.why: One thread per account means no double spending.

quiz.q: A buy limit at ₹412.60 for 200 meets asks of 100 and 250 at ₹412.55 (the 100 is older). What fills?
choices: 100 from the older and 100 from the newer, both at ₹412.55
Nothing, because prices don't match exactly
quiz.why: Price then time, and the resting price wins.

quiz.q: Phones on weak networks cause WebSocket gateways to run out of memory. What is the fix?
choices: Keep only the latest snapshot per symbol per socket, overwriting stale ones
quiz.why: Prices are latest-value-wins, so old ticks can be dropped.

quiz.q: Autoscaling kicks in at 9:20, five minutes after the open spike. What is the better approach?
choices: Scale on a schedule before the open, sized from the busiest recent open plus headroom
quiz.why: The spike arrives at a known second and lasts minutes.

quiz.q: At the open, the order path is overloaded. Which orders should go first?
quiz.why: Someone getting out of a falling stock matters most.

quiz.q: The end-of-day trade file has a fill the broker never recorded. What must happen?
choices: Explain and fix the break before settlement
Wait for the user to complain
quiz.why: Breaks between the trade file and the broker's fills are resolved before T+1 settlement.
